opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think it's actually a really instructive case, and people sometimes draw the wrong lesson from it. The naive read is "the model is dumb, it can't even beat a children's game." But if you watch the runs, the failures mostly aren't about reasoning in the abstract. Claude can tell you what a type matchup is, what the strategy for a gym should be, all of that. Where it struggles is much more mundane: perception and memory over long horizons.

On the perception side, these models weren't really trained to parse pixel-art Game Boy screens. So it'll misread where a door is, think it's standing somewhere it isn't, or walk into the same wall over and over because it doesn't realize it's a wall. A human kid gets that for free because our visual system is incredibly well-tuned for that kind of thing.

Then there's the memory piece, which I find more interesting. The context window fills up, so it has to summarize and write notes to itself, and every time it compresses, it loses information or occasionally hallucinates something into its notes. Then it trusts that note later. So you get these loops where it's convinced it already checked a building, or that some item is somewhere it isn't, and it can spend hours stuck. That's not a lack of intelligence so much as not having a good working memory and not having learned when to doubt its own records.

What's encouraging is that each model generation gets noticeably further, and a lot of the bottlenecks look like things that improve with scale and with training on long-horizon agentic tasks rather than fundamental walls. So I read Pokemon less as "here's the ceiling" and more as a nice, legible benchmark for the exact capabilities that matter for agents doing real work: staying coherent over thousands of steps, noticing when you're stuck, and recovering. When models can just cruise through Pokemon, I think that'll tell you a lot about how close they are to doing multi-day engineering tasks on their own.

r001.rationale: The response says each successive model generation gets noticeably further through Pokémon.

r002.rationale: It identifies both perception and memory as major sources of difficulty, without clearly saying memory-system limitations are the primary cause.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the Pokemon stuff is actually really interesting, and the way I'd interpret it is that it's mostly a memory and long-horizon agency problem rather than an intelligence problem, if that distinction makes sense.

Like, if you watch the stream, Claude isn't confused about what Pokemon is or what it should be doing. It knows it needs to get the gym badges, it knows how the battles work, it can reason about type matchups fine. Where it struggles is stuff like getting stuck in a corner of Mt. Moon for hours, or walking back and forth between the same two rooms, or forgetting that it already tried a particular path. And a lot of that comes down to the fact that it has this very limited context window relative to the task. Every so often the context gets summarized and compressed, and you lose a lot of the texture of what happened. So it's a little like Memento, right? You wake up and you have some notes, but you don't actually have the rich episodic memory of "I was here forty minutes ago and that door was locked."

And I think humans really underrate how much of what we do relies on that kind of continuous memory. A ten-year-old playing Pokemon isn't smarter than Claude in any sort of raw reasoning sense. But they have a persistent model of the world that just keeps updating as they play, and they don't have to re-derive where they are from a screenshot every step.

The other piece, which I think people miss, is the vision side. The game is being presented as a pretty low-resolution screenshot, and the model's spatial understanding of that grid, like which tiles are walkable and which are walls, is genuinely weaker than its language reasoning. So some of what looks like "Claude is being dumb" is actually "Claude can't tell that this is a ledge it can't walk up."

So when I see it struggle, I don't read it as evidence that the model fundamentally can't do agentic tasks. I read it as evidence that the scaffolding, the memory, and the perception are lagging behind the core reasoning. And the encouraging thing is that each generation of model has gotten noticeably further in the game, which suggests those pieces are improvable. It's a nice honest benchmark precisely because it's not something we optimized for. You can't really game it the way you can game a standard eval.

r001.rationale: It says each generation of model has gotten noticeably further in the game.

r002.rationale: It attributes the struggles mostly to memory and long-horizon agency, describing how context compression causes Claude to lose details of prior attempts.

astra-6.text:
I think it highlights the gap between being able to explain what you should do and being able to actually do it over a long horizon. You can ask Claude for a Pokémon strategy and get a very reasonable answer. But playing requires keeping track of where you are, what you’ve tried, and whether your last action actually accomplished what you intended.

And little mistakes compound. If you misunderstand the screen or get confused about your position, you can spend a lot of time acting on that mistaken belief. The important thing is whether you can notice that you’re stuck and revise your understanding.

So I wouldn’t read it as a clean measure of how intelligent the model is. You’re testing the model together with its interface, its memory, and the feedback it gets. But I also wouldn’t dismiss it as just an interface problem. Reliably connecting your reasoning to actions, checking what happened, and recovering from mistakes is a real capability—and it matters for much more than Pokémon.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it highlights the gap between having a lot of knowledge and being able to use it reliably over a long horizon. Pokémon looks simple to us, but you’re continually interpreting a screen, keeping track of where you are, choosing actions, and checking whether those actions did what you expected. A small mistake can send you into a loop.

So I’d be careful about interpreting it as a clean measure of how smart Claude is. You’re testing the model together with its interface, memory, and feedback loop. But I also wouldn’t dismiss it as just an interface problem. Recognizing that you’re stuck, revising your understanding, and trying something different are important parts of intelligence.

The interesting question is what causes a particular failure. Does it not understand what it needs to do? Does it understand but lose track of the plan? Or does it fail to connect its actions to what changes on the screen? Those suggest pretty different things we need to improve.
